1041.event_title: Dadabhai Naoroji publishes Poverty and Un-British Rule in India
1041.event: Dadabhai Naoroji, the Indian nationalist who had served as a British MP, published Poverty and Un-British Rule in India in 1901 while living at Anerley Park in Penge, London. The book was the fullest statement of his drain theory, which held that India had been impoverished by high taxation and by an expensive foreign administration whose costs drained wealth to Britain, and that British policies had contributed to deadly famines.
1041.explanation: Naoroji made Indian poverty itself the measure by which colonial rule was judged, and his drain theory became the basis of the classic Indian nationalist critique of British rule.
1041.tie_back: The kural says nothing is more grievous than poverty except poverty itself, and Naoroji built a lifetime's political argument on the conviction that India's poverty was the affliction beside which all others had to be measured.
1041._accuracy_note: Next-best: the book treats poverty as the supreme ill of a nation, but the kural's point is a reflective comparison of personal sorrows rather than an economic argument.

1042.event_title: Germany's hyperinflation wipes out a lifetime of savings
1042.event: During 1923 the German paper mark collapsed as the government printed ever more banknotes, and by November it took about 4.2 trillion marks to buy a single US dollar. Middle-class Germans who lived on savings, pensions, investments or rents saw the provision they had built up over a lifetime become almost worthless, and the crisis was ended only by the introduction of the Rentenmark late in 1923.
1042.explanation: The hyperinflation reduced respectable, provident families to want almost overnight, and historians link the experience to a lasting loss of trust in money and in the Weimar Republic.
1042.tie_back: The kural calls poverty a wicked thing that robs a person of both this life and the next, and the hyperinflation took from savers at a stroke both their comfort in the present and the security they had stored up for the years ahead.
1042._accuracy_note: Partial fit: it matches the temporal reading of the kural (present and future both lost) rather than the traditional reading in which poverty prevents the giving that earns merit in the next world.

1043.event_title: Debt-ridden Benedict Arnold plots to hand West Point to the British
1043.event: Benedict Arnold, born into a well-respected Connecticut family, had become one of the Continental Army's most celebrated generals, but he and his second wife lived lavishly in Philadelphia and ran deep into debt. After receiving command of the fort at West Point in 1780, he met the British officer Major John Andre on 21 September 1780 to arrange its surrender in return for a large sum of money and a British commission. Andre was captured with incriminating papers, the plot was exposed, and Arnold fled to the British side.
1043.explanation: Historians count Arnold's debts, together with his resentment at being passed over for promotion, among the motives for his betrayal, and his name became a byword for traitor in the United States.
1043.tie_back: The kural warns that the craving born of want destroys at a single stroke a family's old standing and good name, and Arnold's debt-driven treason erased a hero's reputation overnight.
1043._accuracy_note: Strong illustration of sudden ruin of name through financial craving, though Arnold's want came from extravagance rather than destitution and debt was only one of his motives.

1044.event_title: Mozart's letters to Michael Puchberg asking for loans
1044.event: From June 1788, at a hard time for musicians in Vienna, Mozart began writing a series of letters to his friend and fellow Freemason, the merchant Michael Puchberg, asking for money. In one he admitted that he still owed Puchberg eight ducats and could not repay them, yet asked for a hundred gulden more; later letters asked for far larger sums. Puchberg lent smaller amounts again and again, and the appeals continued until a few months before Mozart's death in December 1791.
1044.explanation: The letters show one of the most gifted and cultivated artists of his age reduced by money troubles to repeated, apologetic pleas.
1044.tie_back: The kural says that want breeds, even in the well-born, a weariness from which humbling words come out, and Mozart's pleading letters to Puchberg are a documented case of a refined man pressed into such speech.
1044._accuracy_note: Strong fit for want producing humbling speech; scholars debate how poor Mozart really was, since his recorded earnings in these years were substantial.

1045.place: Brussels and Paris (written at Hauteville House, Guernsey)
1045.event: Victor Hugo, living in exile at Hauteville House on Guernsey, published Les Miserables in 1862, and it was an immediate popular success that was quickly translated into other languages. In its short preface Hugo named the degradation of men through poverty, the ruin of women through hunger and the stunting of children as the problems of the age, and the novel follows the ex-convict Jean Valjean and the impoverished single mother Fantine through a chain of misfortunes that grow out of want.
1045.explanation: The novel made the many-sided suffering of the poor the centre of a work read across the world, and it remains one of the best-known portraits of social injustice in nineteenth-century France.
1045.tie_back: The kural says that within the single affliction of poverty sorrows of every kind gather, and Hugo's preface and story trace exactly that: hunger, prison, outcasting, illness and the ruin of children all rooted in want.
1045._accuracy_note: A reasonable to strong fit for poverty as the matrix of many sorrows, though the event is the publication of a novel rather than a real person's experience.

1046.event_title: The Jarrow March brings a petition of the unemployed to Parliament
1046.place: Jarrow to London, England, United Kingdom
1046.event: After the closure of Palmer's shipyard left most of Jarrow's workforce without jobs, about 200 unemployed men, each medically examined, marched nearly 300 miles to London carrying a petition signed by some 12,000 people asking for new industry. Their MP, Ellen Wilkinson, presented the petition to Parliament on 4 November 1936, but Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin did not meet the marchers, the petition was received without being debated, and the march produced few immediate results.
1046.explanation: The marchers' orderly, well-reasoned plea won public sympathy along the route yet was largely passed over by the government, though the march later came to be seen as a defining event of the 1930s.
1046.tie_back: The kural observes that even sound and well-understood words lose their force when spoken by the poor, and the Jarrow men's carefully argued petition was received in Parliament and left undebated.
1046._accuracy_note: Strong illustration of the poor being heard but not heeded; the government's stated reason was a policy of not encouraging marches rather than open contempt for the speakers.

1047.event_title: Edgar Allan Poe's gambling debts estrange him from his foster father
1047.place: Charlottesville and Richmond, Virginia, United States
1047.event: Edgar Allan Poe, raised in Richmond as the foster son of the merchant John Allan, was sent to the University of Virginia in 1826 with too little money to cover his expenses. When Allan ignored his requests for help, Poe turned to gambling, ran up debts of about 2,000 dollars that Allan refused to pay, and left the university in December 1826. Estranged from Allan and facing his creditors, he left Richmond for Boston in 1827.
1047.explanation: The quarrel over debts incurred through gambling began a lasting breach between Poe and the man who had brought him up.
1047.tie_back: The kural says that want unconnected with virtue makes a person a stranger even to the one who raised him, and Poe's gambling debts turned his foster father against him.
1047._accuracy_note: Partial fit: the estrangement was from a foster father rather than a mother, and Allan's own stinginess helped create the want that led to the gambling.

1048.event: In September 1944 the German occupiers imposed an embargo on food transport to the western Netherlands, and with an exceptionally harsh winter and poor harvests the region slid into famine. People lived on rations of roughly 400 to 800 calories a day and ate grass and tulip bulbs to survive, and about 20,000 people died before liberation in May 1945.
1048.explanation: For months millions of people woke each day not knowing whether they would find enough to eat, and the famine left lasting effects on the health of survivors and their children.
1048.tie_back: The kural gives the voice of the poor man who asks each morning whether yesterday's crushing want will come again today, and the Hunger Winter was a whole population living that dread day after day.
1048._accuracy_note: Reasonable to strong fit for daily dread of returning want, though the famine was caused by war and blockade rather than ordinary poverty.

1049.event_title: George Orwell publishes Down and Out in Paris and London
1049.event: George Orwell's first book, Down and Out in Paris and London, published in 1933, recounts in lightly fictionalised form his own time living among the poor. In Paris he lived in a slum and worked as a hotel dishwasher, and in London and on the roads of England he lived as a tramp, queuing for a bed in the casual wards and lodging houses where a mug of tea, a piece of bread and a blanket were all that was offered.
1049.explanation: The book showed readers from the inside how destitution governs every hour of a poor person's day and night, and it helped change how homelessness was discussed in Britain.
1049.tie_back: The kural says a person may somehow sleep in fire but never in the midst of want, and Orwell's account shows the destitute spending their nights in anxious search of a place to lie down.
1049._accuracy_note: Next-best: the book documents the restless nights of the destitute, but the sources consulted do not single out sleeplessness, which is the kural's precise image.

1050.event_title: Gandhi adopts the loincloth at Madurai
1050.event: On his tour of South India in 1921, while urging people to boycott foreign cloth, Gandhi met many who said they were too poor to buy khadi to replace what they wore. In Madurai on 22 September 1921 he gave up his shirt and cap and adopted the simple loincloth (some accounts say dhoti and shawl), explaining that he hesitated to advise anything he was not prepared to follow himself and wanted to make the change easier for those who could not afford new clothes.
1050.explanation: Gandhi chose to reduce his own needs to the level of the poorest rather than ask more of them, and the simple dress became his lasting symbol.
1050.tie_back: The kural says that those who have nothing should embrace full renunciation rather than linger as a burden on others, and Gandhi's decision at Madurai was a voluntary renunciation that identified him with India's poorest.
1050._accuracy_note: Next-best: Gandhi was not destitute and his act was a chosen simplicity, so it echoes the kural's call to renunciation only loosely.
